P1.evidence: Same opener the rep uses everywhere: 'I've seen your application, but to be honest, I'm kind of old school, and I would love to hear it from you and get into more detail.' The application is referenced but deliberately not read back, so P1a is partial. The four-part frame — where you are, where you want to go, what's in the way, what you need — was never set, and this is the call in the batch where that omission has a traceable cost: without 'what you need' being framed as today's decision, the prospect arrived believing 'usually first calls are introductions' and said so at the close. Agreement was sought only as a trailing 'Cool.' and answered 'So, yeah, no, excellent.' The open question ran properly.

P2.evidence: The best baseline in the batch. Work was asked properly and pursued through commute and daily movement: 'what do you do for a living? Do you actually, like, sit in front of the computer most of the day?' then 'How do you commute to your work?' and 'during the day, do you move around or is it that you're sitting all day'. Injuries asked and followed up twice — 'Do you have any injuries or anything that limits your movements?' then a specific probe for lower back and hip stiffness. Diet asked as an open walkthrough: 'Could you walk me through a basic meal plan?' Sleep asked with the quality follow-up: 'How is your sleep?' and 'Do you feel rested when you wake up?' Age, height and weight were all volunteered unprompted while the rep listened, so P2a scores miss despite the data existing. Health conditions are partial — cholesterol came from the prospect, but the rep did follow up well with 'how about the other blood work that you had done? Like, how about testosterone level?' Training week and results are partial: cricket and cycling were drawn out, but no current weekly pattern or actual days trained was ever pinned down. Energy through the day was only ever inferred from stamina in cricket.

P3.evidence: The aesthetic question was asked cleanly — 'Any tangible goal in terms of looks?' — producing 'I've never been in a shape that I would like to be... more defined. Like, more athletic.' The bridge question also ran, in near-scripted form: 'in your own words, like what's the biggest reason you want to actually do this right now, like what's the big why behind that' — which surfaced heart health and the six-month cholesterol re-test. From there the phase stops working. The rep never asked who else it impacts; he asserted it himself ('you're going to be leading by example', 'my dad, the superhero dad that you're going to become') and then delivered a two-minute monologue about other clients' confidence and relationships improving. The prospect's agreement to all of it was passive — 'Yeah, no, I agree, I agree. That's an additional thing' — which is a tell that the why was supplied rather than surfaced. Reflect-back landed only at the structural level: 'So, like, you need a structure?' / 'Yes. Yes.' Never at the emotional level the phase exists for.

P4.evidence: The gap got named, which is the point of the phase, but the prospect did the work unprompted: 'I just never had someone give me a routine and show me like, here's what you need... I want someone to tell you, here's exactly what you need to do in order for you to achieve this.' The rep reflected it back correctly as structure. What he never asked was the direct sequence — no 'what have you tried before', no 'what happened with that', and critically no 'why do you feel it didn't stick'. The prior gym membership, the personal trainer and the five-to-six-month cycling habit all surfaced incidentally, and the obvious root cause sitting in plain view — two children arriving and ending the habit — was never named, tested or used.

P5.evidence: Phase never run. No two-year question, no settle question, no 'why not', no line in the sand. The closest thing was a forward-looking benefit statement attached to nutrition — 'If you want to play the long-term game and be healthy, and you want to be healthy for your kids when they grow up, we need to have that covered too' — which frames a reward, not a cost of inaction. This is the direct cause of the outcome: with no consequence banked, there was nothing to return to when the prospect asked for time, and the rep had only a $100 deposit to reach for.

P6.evidence: A commitment check did run before the offer: 'my last question is, if we can figure out all the details, are you fully committed to showing up and doing the work?' answered 'Yes. Yes, I am.' That is the all-in question in weakened form — it asks about effort, not about reasons not to proceed, so P6b is partial. The belief question was never asked before presenting; the rep only got to it after the objection had already landed, at 00:48:25 — 'How do you feel about this actually? Do you feel like this can get you to your goals?' — drawing a hedged 'I think so. I think so.' P6c fails outright: the script says return to Phase 5 when hesitation surfaces, and when it surfaced the rep instead asked for a deposit and then conceded the call.

P11.evidence: A close was attempted, so the phase applies. The rep announced it — 'let's get through the agreement and the payment. And I'll send you in the chat the payment link' — and got no further; no link was sent and no payment taken. The Trevor slot for Tuesday the 28th at 3:15pm Pacific was booked and then explicitly released ('you don't have to book anything for next week'), so P11b is partial. Agreement, welcome email, Skool and onboarding form were never reached. The rep also declined a direct request to send the agreement and payment link by email — 'usually what we do is we just take it, cover it over the meeting, because I need to onboard you, and that's the procedure' — which removed the one path that might have preserved the sale asynchronously.

objection_plays.detail: Clear trigger, stated three times: 'I just wanted to kind of do some research before I commit to this, you know, 6K', 'I need to really look into it before I commit', 'I do want to take the time and get back to you.' The rep ran the opening move — 'Do you feel like this can get you to your goals?' — and got 'I think so.' He then abandoned the play. He never asked the follow-up 'What makes you feel it can?', never asked the pivotal 'So what's actually coming up that's preventing you from getting started?', never used 'Thinking isn't the problem. Deciding is', never used the different-decision or identity moves, and never ran the final 'are you sure, nothing else keeping you from being 100% in?' Instead he validated the delay outright — 'Sure thing. Go do your due diligence' — and then, having given permission, tried to reattach commitment with a $100 deposit. The order is backwards: the play should have run to completion before any concession.

The underlying objection was certainty about the provider rather than about himself — 'I want to make sure this is the right path', 'I still like to understand what other people are saying about this six-month program, other than what you guys said.' Exactly one OE move ran, and it ran well: 'you can read all the reviews that you want, but eventually how actually you will know if you never actually tried it for yourself on your body.' That is the 'how will you know if you never actually try' close. None of the surrounding structure ran — no 'would it be fair to say you're looking for certainty', no pleasure-versus-pain frame, no bridge, no plane, no burned-before. One move landed in isolation and did not carry.

A soft money trigger — a discount request ('There's no promotion for a new person, or any of that') and a request not to pay upfront. The rep handled the discount request correctly and better than anywhere else in this batch: 'there is no, like, discount on the price itself. But we can structure the payment.' Price held. But the play proper never ran: no isolation, no should-versus-how frame, and no financial picture at all — no cash on hand, no monthly surplus, no cards, no available credit, no investments. Arguably defensible here, since the prospect twice said money was not the issue ('I don't mind paying that'), which is precisely what the isolation move exists to establish and which the rep therefore got for free.

SCRIPT GAP — expectation mismatch about the purpose of the call. The prospect stated plainly that he had not understood this was a decision call: 'it's not that you, I have to pay on the first call. Usually first calls are introductions, explaining what it is and all that stuff' and 'I was hoping this first call would be to really understand what it is.' There is no scripted response because P1's four-part frame is supposed to prevent it upstream. The rep converted it into self-blame ('it looks I haven't done my job properly if you don't have clarity until now') and then asked what was unclear, which cannot work — the issue was not clarity about the programme but about the call. This is a setter and framing failure, not a rep failure at the objection, and it should be fixed in P1 and in the setter handoff.

SCRIPT GAP — demand for independent third-party proof. 'I'm just more of an online thing, not just general public websites, they're saying.' The playbook has no move for a buyer who discounts first-party testimonials on principle, and the company appears to have no independent review presence to point at. The rep could only re-offer company-supplied material — the testimonials already sent and a client's before-and-after photos — which is the same source the prospect had just discounted. Worth escalating as a marketing gap rather than a coaching note.

notes: The strongest discovery in the batch — work, injuries, diet and sleep all genuinely asked — attached to the weakest closing sequence. Phase 5 never ran, so when the prospect asked for time there was no consequence to return to and the rep skipped from one incomplete OA move straight to permission-giving. Two fixable process errors: set the four-part frame in P1 so the prospect knows a decision is on the table, and refusing to email the agreement removed the only asynchronous path to the sale. Do not coach this as a price loss — he said twice he was fine paying $6,000 and had already bought the kettlebells.
